steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Key differences between DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid)

1. Sugar component  
   • DNA: Deoxyribose (lacks an –OH group on the 2′ carbon).  
   • RNA: Ribose (has an –OH group on the 2′ carbon).  
   → The extra –OH in RNA makes it more chemically reactive and less stable than DNA.

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA: Adenine (A), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C), Thymine (T).  
   • RNA: A, G, C, Uracil (U) in place of thymine.  
   → Uracil pairs with adenine during transcription and translation.

3. Strandedness & 3-D structure  
   • DNA: Typically double-stranded helix (antiparallel strands held by A–T and G–C hydrogen bonds).  
   • RNA: Usually single-stranded, but can fold back on itself to form hairpins and complex 3-D shapes (tRNA, rRNA, ribozymes).

4. Function  
   • DNA: Long-term storage of genetic information; blueprint passed from cell to cell and parent to offspring.  
   • RNA: Versatile working molecule. Major roles:  
     – mRNA: conveys genetic code from DNA to ribosome.  
     – rRNA: core component of ribosomes, catalyzes peptide bond formation.  
     – tRNA: brings amino acids to ribosome.  
     – Regulatory RNAs (miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA) control gene expression.  
     – Some viruses (e.g., influenza, SARS-CoV-2) use RNA as their genome.

5. Location in eukaryotic cells  
   • DNA: Mostly in nucleus (chromosomes); also in mitochondria/chloroplasts.  
   • RNA: Synthesized in nucleus but functions mainly in cytoplasm (ribosomes, ER, etc.); many specialized RNAs also stay in nucleus or other organelles.

6. Stability & lifespan  
   • DNA: Highly stable; protective histones and double helix shield bases; can last decades or millennia (fossils).  
   • RNA: Short-lived; single strand and 2′-OH make it prone to hydrolysis; cellular RNases degrade it minutes-to-hours after use.

7. Replication vs. transcription  
   • DNA duplicates via DNA polymerases during S phase, producing identical duplexes with proofreading.  
   • RNA synthesized from DNA template by RNA polymerases during transcription; error rate higher, no full-genome copying.

8. Repair mechanisms  
   • DNA: Multiple elaborate repair pathways (mismatch, base-excision, nucleotide-excision, double-strand break repair).  
   • RNA: Limited repair; generally degraded and resynthesized if damaged.

9. Quantitative ratio in cell  
   • DNA mass is constant for a given genome.  
   • RNA mass fluctuates with cell activity; rRNA is 80-90 % of total RNA.

10. Evolutionary note  
   • RNA is thought to predate DNA (the “RNA world” hypothesis): it can store information and catalyze reactions (ribozymes). DNA likely evolved later as a more stable repository once cells needed larger genomes.

Mnemonic summary  
D-NA: Double, Deoxy, Durable, Data storage.  
R-NA: Ribose, Reactive, Random shapes, Regulatory, Relay of information.
